explain.narrative:
## Core idea
A readable text file object exposes methods for consuming text. `read()` returns a string, `readline()` returns one line, and iteration processes lines lazily. Reading advances the stream position, so a second read at the end usually returns an empty string unless the stream is repositioned.

## Syntax and behaviour
Use `file.read(size)` for all or part of the remaining content, `file.readline()` for one line, or `for line in file:` for line-by-line processing. `seek()` changes the position on seekable streams; `tell()` reports the current position.

## Rules and practical guidance
Large files should usually be processed line by line rather than loaded completely. Text mode decodes bytes using the selected encoding. Strip only the line ending or whitespace you intend to remove; `strip()` also removes spaces and tabs at both ends.

## Example walkthroughs
The five examples below use deterministic in-memory streams or automatically cleaned temporary directories. Their outputs are designed to be reproducible in the course validator.

## Common mistakes
- Choosing a destructive mode when existing content must be preserved.
- Assuming paths are relative to the script file rather than the process working directory.
- Forgetting that text and binary streams accept different data types.
- Building CSV or JSON by manually concatenating strings.
- Ignoring exceptions caused by missing paths, permissions, invalid encodings or malformed data.

## Best practices
Use the standard library, explicit UTF-8 for text, context managers for resources, narrow exception handling and validation at application boundaries. Keep untrusted input within an explicitly approved data area.

examples.title: Read all remaining text
examples.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('red\nblue') as file:
    print(repr(file.read()))
examples.explanation: read() returns the remaining text as one string; repr makes the embedded newline visible.

examples.title: Read one line at a time
examples.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('one\ntwo\n') as file:
    print(repr(file.readline()))
    print(repr(file.readline()))
examples.explanation: readline() includes the line-ending character when it is present.

examples.title: Iterate through lines
examples.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('A
B
C
') as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.rstrip('
'))
examples.explanation: File iteration reads one line at a time, avoiding the need to store the entire file in memory.

examples.title: Read a bounded number of characters
examples.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('abcdef') as file:
    print(file.read(3))
    print(file.tell())
examples.explanation: The size argument limits the number of characters returned in text mode; tell reports the current stream position.

examples.title: Return to the beginning before rereading
examples.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('data') as file:
    print(file.read())
    file.seek(0)
    print(file.read(2))
examples.explanation: seek(0) moves the stream position back to the start, allowing a second read.

questions.prompt: What does read() return in text mode?
questions.answer: The remaining text as a string
options: The remaining text as a string
questions.explanation: Text-mode read returns a string containing the remaining text.

questions.prompt: What does readline() normally retain when present?
questions.explanation: readline returns one line and includes its newline when present.

questions.prompt: Why iterate over a large file?
questions.explanation: Iteration avoids loading the entire file into memory at once.

questions.prompt: What does seek(0) do on a seekable stream?
questions.answer: Moves the position to the beginning
options: Moves the position to the beginning
questions.explanation: Offset zero from the start returns the stream position to the beginning.
